english.heading: Seeds and Seed Sovereignty
body: Seed is where the next season begins.
When your household can save, store and share good seed, it carries more than a crop forward. It also carries the freedom to choose.
In this lesson, you will follow seed from the parent plant to the packet, the germination test and a neighbour’s hand.
Think about the crops in your area. Which ones do you already save seed from? Which seed do you buy? Which seed do you exchange?
Try to name at least one crop whose seed is already being saved in your area.

heading.text: Mbeu na Maanḓa kha Mbeu (seed sovereignty)
heading.backTranslation: Seed and Power in Seed (seed sovereignty)

body.text: Khalaṅwaha i tevhelaho i thoma nga mbeu.
body.backTranslation: The coming season begins with seed.

body.text: Musi muṱa waṋu u tshi kona u vhulunga, u vhea na u kovhelana mbeu yavhuḓi, u isa phanḓa zwinzhi u fhira tshilimiwa (crop) fhedzi. Nahone u isa phanḓa na mbofholowo ya u nanga.
body.backTranslation: When your household can keep, store and share good seed, it goes further than only the crop. And it carries on the freedom of choosing.

body.text: Kha ngudo iyi, ni ḓo tevhela mbeu u bva kha tshimela tsha mubebi u ya kha pakete, kha mulingo wa u mela (germination test), na u swika tshanḓani tsha muhura.
body.backTranslation: In this lesson, you will follow seed from the parent plant to the packet, to the test of sprouting (germination test), and to the yard of the neighbour.

body.text: Humbulani nga zwilimiwa (crops) zwa henefho. Ndi zwifhio zwine na vhulunga mbeu yazwo zwino? Ndi mbeu ifhio ine na i renga? Ndi mbeu ifhio ine na i kovhelana na vhaṅwe?
body.backTranslation: Think of local crops. Which ones do you keep the seed of now? Which seed do you buy? Which seed do you share with others?

body.text: Lingedzani u bula dzina ḽa tshilimiwa (crop) tshithihi kana zwinzhi, tshine mbeu yatsho i khou vhulungwa zwino henefho.
body.backTranslation: Try to open the name of one crop or more, whose seed is being kept locally now.

english.heading: Why Saving Seed Matters
body: Saving seed does not mean rejecting all bought seed. It means building practical choices.
Each crop you learn to save well removes one repeated purchase. It also begins a local record of what performs well in your soil and your season.
Think about the seed you buy again and again. Which repeated seed purchase costs your household the most each year?
Choose one crop from your planting list. Make it your practical starting point for seed saving. Do not try to save everything at once.

heading.text: Ndeme ya U Vhulunga Mbeu

body.text: U vhulunga mbeu a zwi ambi u hana mbeu yoṱhe yo rengwaho. Zwi amba u vha na khetho dzi re na mushumo.
body.backTranslation: Keeping seed does not mean refusing all seed that is bought. It means having choices that work.

body.text: Tshilimiwa tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe tshine na guda u vhulunga mbeu yatsho zwavhuḓi tshi ni thusa uri ni si tsha renga mbeu yatsho hafhu na hafhu. Nahone ni thoma u ṅwala zwine zwa aluwa zwavhuḓi mavuni aṋu na nga khalaṅwaha yaṋu.
body.backTranslation: Each crop whose seed you learn to keep well helps you not to buy its seed again and again. And you begin to record what grows well in your soils and in your season.

body.text: Humbulani nga mbeu ine na i renga hafhu na hafhu. Ndi mbeu ifhio ine muṱa waṋu wa shumisa tshelede nnzhi u fhira dzoṱhe u i renga ṅwaha muṅwe na muṅwe?
body.backTranslation: Think of seed that you buy again and again. Which seed does your household use the most money of all to buy every year?

body.text: Nangani tshilimiwa tshithihi kha mutevhe waṋu wa u zwala. Kha tshi vhe mathomo aṋu a u vhulunga mbeu. Ni songo lingedza u vhulunga zwoṱhe nga tshifhinga tshithihi.
body.backTranslation: Choose one crop in your planting list. Let it be your beginning of keeping seed. Do not try to keep all at one time.

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: This lesson ends with a working seed store, not a list of facts.
You will make four decisions.
What will you save?
How will you process it?
How will you protect it?
And how will you know it is still alive before you depend on it?
Which of these four decisions is least familiar to you?
Say them again in your own words: select, process, protect and verify.

heading.text: Zwine Na Ḓo Guda

body.text: Ngudo iyi i fhela nga fhethu ha u vhulunga mbeu hu shumaho, hu si mutevhe wa mafhungo.
body.backTranslation: This lesson ends with a working place of keeping seed, not a list of information.

body.text: Ni ḓo ita khetho nṋa.
body.backTranslation: You will make four choices.

body.text: Ni ḓo vhulunga mini?
body.backTranslation: What will you keep?

body.text: Ni ḓo zwi lugisa hani?
body.backTranslation: How will you prepare it?

body.text: Ni ḓo zwi tsireledza hani?
body.backTranslation: How will you protect it?

body.text: Nahone ni ḓo ḓivha hani uri mbeu i kha ḓi tshila ni sa athu u ḓitika ngayo?
body.backTranslation: And how will you know that the seed is still alive before depending on it?

body.text: Ndi ifhio kha khetho idzi nṋa ine na i ḓivha zwiṱuku u fhira dziṅwe?
body.backTranslation: Which of these four choices do you know less than the others?

body.text: Zwi ambeni hafhu nga maipfi aṋu: nanga, lugisa, tsireledza na khwaṱhisedza (select, process, protect, verify).
body.backTranslation: Say it again in your own words: select, process, protect and verify (select, process, protect, verify).

english.heading: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed
body: Open-pollinated seed is not magic.
A stable variety can produce similar generations when it is properly isolated or self-pollinated.
F1 seed usually remains alive. But the next generation separates into different combinations of the parent traits.
The problem is unpredictability, not failure to germinate.
Think about one small bed on your own plot. Why could unpredictable plants be a risk when space is limited?
If you have seed packets, check whether they are marked open-pollinated or F1. Which would you choose for saving dependable seed?
Remember: the next F1 generation varies. It does not automatically die.

heading.text: Mbeu ya Open-Pollinated na Mbeu ya F1

body.text: Mbeu ya open-pollinated a si tshithu tshi mangadzaho (magic).
body.backTranslation: Open-pollinated seed is not something amazing (magic).

body.text: Stable variety i nga bveledza mirafho i fanaho musi yo khethekanywa zwavhuḓi (isolated) kana i tshi ita self-pollination.
body.backTranslation: A stable variety can produce generations that are alike when it has been separated well (isolated) or it is doing self-pollination.

body.text: Mbeu ya F1 kanzhi i a tshila. Fhedzi murafho u tevhelaho u a fhambana: zwivhumbeo (traits) zwa vhabebi zwi ṱangana nga nḓila dzo fhambanaho.
body.backTranslation: F1 seed usually lives. But the next generation differs: the traits of the parents combine in different ways.

body.text: Thaidzo ndi u sa ḓivha zwine zwa ḓo bvelela, hu si u sa mela ha mbeu.
body.backTranslation: The problem is not knowing what will come out, not the seed failing to sprout.

body.text: Humbulani nga bede ḽiṱuku ḽithihi kha tsimu yaṋu. Ndi ngani zwimela zwine na sa ḓivhi uri zwi ḓo vha hani zwi nga vha khombo musi fhethu hu si hunzhi?
body.backTranslation: Think of one small bed in your field. Why could plants whose outcome you do not know be a danger when the place is not big?

body.text: Arali ni na pakete dza mbeu, sedzani arali dzo ṅwalwa open-pollinated kana F1. Ni nga nanga ifhio u vhulunga mbeu i fulufhedzeaho?
body.backTranslation: If you have seed packets, look whether they are written open-pollinated or F1. Which can you choose for keeping reliable seed?

body.text: Humbulani: murafho u tevhelaho wa F1 u a fhambana. A zwi ambi uri mbeu i ḓo fa.
body.backTranslation: Remember: the next generation of F1 differs. It does not say that the seed will die.

english.heading: Watch: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed
body: Watch both sides.
Both kinds of seed germinate.
Open-pollinated seed produces similar plants when the variety is stable and pollination is properly managed.
Seed saved from an F1 plant also germinates. But its next generation varies. Some plants may be tall. Others may be short. Their vigour and yield may differ.
Ask yourself what this means when choosing seed to save.
If you understand the difference, you can explain it in one sentence: both germinate, but the next F1 generation is unpredictable.

heading.text: Sedzani: Mbeu ya Open-Pollinated na Mbeu ya F1
heading.backTranslation: Look: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed

body.text: Sedzani thungo dzoṱhe mbili.
body.backTranslation: Look at both sides.

body.text: Mbeu dzoṱhe mbili dzi a mela.
body.backTranslation: Both seeds sprout.

body.text: Mbeu ya open-pollinated i bveledza zwimela zwi fanaho musi lushaka (variety) lu tshi vha stable nahone pollination i tshi langwa zwavhuḓi.
body.backTranslation: Seed of open-pollinated produces plants that are alike when the kind (variety) is/becomes stable and also pollination is being managed well.

body.text: Mbeu yo vhulungwaho kha tshimela tsha F1 i a mela na yone. Fhedzi murafho wayo u tevhelaho u a fhambana. Zwiṅwe zwimela zwi nga vha zwilapfu. Zwiṅwe zwi nga vha zwipfufhi. Maanḓa azwo (vigour) na khaṋo (yield) zwi nga fhambana.
body.backTranslation: Seed kept from an F1 plant also sprouts. But its next generation differs. Some plants may be tall. Some may be short. Their strength (vigour) and yield may differ.

body.text: Humbulani uri hezwi zwi amba mini musi ni tshi nanga mbeu ine na ḓo i vhulunga.
body.backTranslation: Think what this means when you choose seed that you will keep.

body.text: Arali ni tshi pfesesa phambano, ni nga i ṱalutshedza nga u pfufhifhadza: dzoṱhe dzi a mela, fhedzi a zwi ḓivhei uri murafho u tevhelaho wa F1 u ḓo vha hani.
body.backTranslation: If you understand the difference, you can explain it briefly: all sprout, but it is not known how the next generation of F1 will be.

english.heading: Seed Sovereignty
body: Seed sovereignty does not live in a slogan.
It lives in a dry packet, a written record and knowledge of how the seed behaves.
Your household begins it. Neighbours extend it. The seasons make the local seed collection more useful.
Which seed does your household already save best?
Draw a small map of the homes near you. Beside each home, write one crop that household could bring to a seed exchange.
Sovereignty needs three things: usable seed, written information and exchange.

heading.text: Maanḓa kha Mbeu (seed sovereignty)

body.text: Maanḓa kha mbeu (seed sovereignty) a a dzuli kha slogan.
body.backTranslation: Seed sovereignty does not stay in a slogan.

body.text: A dzula kha pakete yo omaho, kha zwo ṅwalwaho na kha nḓivho ya uri mbeu i ita hani.
body.backTranslation: It stays in a dry packet, in what is written down and in knowledge of how seed behaves.

body.text: Muṱa waṋu u a thoma. Vhahura vha a andadza. Khalaṅwaha dzi tshi ya, mbeu dzo kuvhanganywaho henefho dzi vha na mushumo muhulwane.
body.backTranslation: Your household begins. Neighbours spread it. As years go, seed gathered locally becomes of great use.

body.text: Ndi mbeu ifhio ine muṱa waṋu wa i vhulunga zwavhuḓi u fhira dzoṱhe zwino?
body.backTranslation: Which seed does your household keep well most of all now?

body.text: Olani mapa muṱuku wa miṱa i re tsini na inwi. Tsini ha muṱa muṅwe na muṅwe, ṅwalani tshilimiwa tshithihi tshine muṱa uyo wa nga tshi ḓisa kha u kovhelana mbeu (seed exchange).
body.backTranslation: Draw a small map of households that are near you. Near each household, write one crop that that household could bring to a seed exchange.

body.text: Maanḓa kha mbeu a ṱoḓa zwithu zwiraru: mbeu ine ya nga shumiswa, mafhungo o ṅwalwaho na u kovhelana.
body.backTranslation: Seed sovereignty needs three things: seed that can be used, information that is written down, and sharing.

english.heading: Watch: Household Seed Network
body: Well-saved seed becomes more powerful when it is known and shared.
Watch one household begin by saving seed well from one crop. Dry seed goes into clean packets. Some packets move to neighbouring homes. The neighbours share different seed in return.
By the end, each household holds more varieties than it had before.
Think about which seed you could share and which seed you might receive from a neighbour. Seed moves. Knowledge and trust must move with it.

heading.text: Sedzani: U Kovhelana Mbeu Vhukati ha Miṱa

body.text: Mbeu yo vhulungwaho zwavhuḓi i vha na maanḓa manzhi musi i tshi ḓivhiwa nahone i tshi kovhelwa.
body.backTranslation: Seed that is well kept has much power when it is known and when it is shared.

body.text: Sedzani muṱa muthihi u tshi thoma nga u vhulunga mbeu zwavhuḓi kha tshilimiwa tshithihi. Mbeu yo omaho i dzhena kha pakete dzo kunaho. Dziṅwe pakete dzi ya miṱani i re tsini. Vhahura na vhone vha kovhela mbeu yo fhambanaho.
body.backTranslation: Look at one household beginning by keeping seed well of one crop. Dry seed goes into clean packets. Some packets go to households that are near. Neighbours also share different seed.

body.text: Mafheleloni, muṱa muṅwe na muṅwe u vha na tshaka nnzhi (varieties) u fhira dze wa vha nadzo mathomoni.
body.backTranslation: In the end, each household has many kinds (varieties) more than it had at the beginning.

body.text: Humbulani nga mbeu ine na nga i kovhela vhaṅwe na mbeu ine na nga i wana kha muhura. Mbeu i a tshimbila. Nḓivho na fulufhelo zwi fanela u tshimbila nayo.
body.backTranslation: Think of seed that you could share with others and seed that you could get from a neighbour. Seed travels. Knowledge and trust must travel with it.

english.heading: Select Several Parent Plants
body: The largest fruit is not always the best seed parent.
Look at the whole plant.
Was it healthy?
Did it mature at the right time?
Was it true to type?
Save from several good plants, especially in cross-pollinated crops. This prevents the next generation from coming from only one parent.
What would make you reject a seed plant even if its fruit were large?
Go to your own plot. Point out the plants you would select and the plants you would reject. Choose several healthy, true-to-type plants. Reject diseased plants and those that are not true to type.

heading.text: Nangani Zwimela Zwinzhi zwa Vhabebi

body.text: Mutshelo muhulu u fhira yoṱhe a u ambi tshifhinga tshoṱhe uri tshimela tshawo ndi mubebi wa khwine wa mbeu.
body.backTranslation: The biggest fruit does not always mean that its plant is the best parent of seed.

body.text: Lavhelesani tshimela tshoṱhe.
body.backTranslation: Look at the whole plant.

body.text: Tsho vha tshi na mutakalo?
body.backTranslation: Was it healthy?

body.text: Tsho vhibva nga tshifhinga tsho teaho?
body.backTranslation: Did it ripen at the correct time?

body.text: Tsho vha tshi fana na lushaka lwatsho (true to type)?
body.backTranslation: Was it like its variety (true to type)?

body.text: Vhulungani mbeu kha zwimela zwinzhi zwavhuḓi, nga maanḓa kha zwilimiwa zwa cross-pollinated. Izwi zwi thivhela uri murafho u tevhelaho u bve kha mubebi muthihi fhedzi.
body.backTranslation: Keep seed from many good plants, especially from cross-pollinated crops. This prevents the next generation from coming from only one parent.

body.text: Ndi mini zwine zwa nga ita uri ni hane tshimela tsha mbeu naho mutshelo watsho u muhulu?
body.backTranslation: What could make you reject a seed plant even though its fruit is big?

body.text: Yani kha tsimu yaṋu. Sumbedzani zwimela zwine na ḓo zwi nanga na zwine na ḓo zwi hana. Nangani zwimela zwinzhi zwi re na mutakalo zwi fanaho na lushaka lwazwo. Hanani zwimela zwo lwalaho na zwi sa fani na lushaka lwazwo.
body.backTranslation: Go to your field. Show the plants that you will choose and those that you will reject. Choose many healthy plants that are like their variety. Reject plants that were sick and that are not like their variety.

english.heading: Control Pollination
body: Some crops mostly self-pollinate. A small garden can therefore keep the variety similar.
Crops pollinated by wind or insects can cross over long distances.
The distance needed depends on the crop, the place and the purpose of the seed. Do not promise varietal purity until you have checked the crop.
How can you separate two varieties without using distance?
You can plant them at different times so they do not flower together. You can also control pollination by hand or with covers.
Remember the three tools: distance, flowering time or controlled pollination.

heading.text: Langani Pollination

body.text: Zwiṅwe zwilimiwa (crops) kanzhi zwi ita self-pollination. Ngauralo, tsimu ṱhukhu i nga ita uri lushaka (variety) lu dzule lu tshi fana.
body.backTranslation: Some crops (crops) often do self-pollination. Therefore, a small field can cause that the kind (variety) keeps being alike.

body.text: Zwilimiwa zwine pollen yazwo ya hwalwa nga muya kana nga zwikhokhonono (insects) zwi nga ṱangana (cross) naho zwi kule vhukuma.
body.backTranslation: Crops whose pollen is carried by wind or by insects (insects) can meet/mix (cross) even though they are very far.

body.text: Tshikhala (distance) tshi ṱoḓeaho tshi ḓitika nga tshilimiwa (crop), fhethu na ndivho ya mbeu. Ni songo fulufhedzisa varietal purity ni sa athu u sedza tshilimiwa.
body.backTranslation: The distance needed depends on the crop, the place and the purpose of the seed. Do not promise varietal purity before looking at the crop.

body.text: Ni nga fhambanya hani tshaka mbili ni sa shumisi tshikhala (distance)?
body.backTranslation: How can you separate two kinds without using distance?

body.text: Ni nga dzi zwala nga zwifhinga zwo fhambanaho uri dzi songo vha na maluvha nga tshifhinga tshithihi. Nahone ni nga langa pollination nga zwanḓa kana nga u fukedza maluvha (covers).
body.backTranslation: You can plant them at different times so that they not have flowers at one time. And also you can manage pollination by hands or by covering the flowers (covers).

body.text: Humbulani zwishumiswa zwiraru: tshikhala (distance), tshifhinga tsha maluvha kana pollination yo langwaho.
body.backTranslation: Think about three things used/tools: space (distance), time of flowers or pollination that has been managed.

english.heading: Watch: Self-Pollination and Crossing
body: Follow the path of the pollen.
In self-pollination, pollen moves within one flower from the part that produces it to the part that receives it. This often helps the variety remain similar.
In a maize field, wind carries pollen from the tassels to the silks. If two varieties are close together and flower at the same time, they can cross.
Think about how distance or different flowering times could prevent that on your own plot.

heading.text: Sedzani: Self-Pollination na Crossing

body.text: Tevhelani nḓila ya pollen.
body.backTranslation: Follow the path of pollen.

body.text: Kha self-pollination, pollen i tshimbila ngomu ha luvha luthihi i bva kha tshipiḓa tshine tsha i bveledza i ya kha tshipiḓa tshine tsha i ṱanganedza. Izwi kanzhi zwi thusa uri lushaka lu dzule lu tshi fana.
body.backTranslation: In self-pollination, pollen travels inside one flower, it comes from the part which produces it, it goes to the part which receives it. These often help that the kind keeps being alike.

body.text: Kha tsimu ya mavhele, muya u hwala pollen u bva kha tassels u ya kha silks. Arali tshaka mbili dzi tshi vha tsini nahone dzi na maluvha nga tshifhinga tshithihi, dzi nga ṱangana (cross).
body.backTranslation: In a field of maize, wind carries pollen from the tassels to the silks. If two kinds are near and they have flowers at one time, they can meet/mix (cross).

body.text: Humbulani uri tshikhala (distance) kana zwifhinga zwo fhambanaho zwa maluvha zwi nga thivhela hani izwo kha tsimu yaṋu.
body.backTranslation: Think how distance or different flowering times could prevent those in your field.

english.heading: Dry and Wet Processing
body: There are two broad ways to process seed.
Dry seed matures in a pod, head or cob. It is collected when fully mature.
Seed inside a fleshy fruit must first be separated from the flesh.
Brief fermentation is especially useful for tomato seed. It is not a rule for every wet-seeded crop.
Think about the crops in your area. Which fit the dry method? Which fit the wet method?
If you have seed or fruit nearby, sort the examples into these two types. Explain the difference by describing what the seed is like at harvest.

heading.text: U Lugisa Mbeu nga Nḓila ya u Oma na ya Maḓi
heading.backTranslation: Preparing Seed in the Dry and the Wet Way

body.text: Hu na nḓila mbili khulwane dza u lugisa mbeu.
body.backTranslation: There are two big ways of preparing seed.

body.text: Mbeu yo omaho i vhibva ngomu ha pod, head kana cob. I kuvhanganywa musi yo vhibva zwavhuḓi.
body.backTranslation: Dry seed ripens inside a pod, head or cob. It is gathered when it is fully ripe.

body.text: Mbeu i re ngomu ha mutshelo u re na nama (fleshy fruit) i fanela u thoma u fhambanywa na nama.
body.backTranslation: Seed that is inside a fruit that has flesh (fleshy fruit) must first be separated from the flesh.

body.text: Fermentation ya tshifhinganyana i thusa nga maanḓa kha mbeu ya tamatisi. A si mulayo kha zwilimiwa zwoṱhe zwa mbeu dza maḓi (wet-seeded).
body.backTranslation: Short fermentation helps especially with tomato seed. It is not a rule for all wet-seeded crops.

body.text: Humbulani nga zwilimiwa zwa henefho. Ndi zwifhio zwi fanelaho nḓila ya u oma? Ndi zwifhio zwi fanelaho nḓila ya maḓi?
body.backTranslation: Think of local crops. Which suit the dry way? Which suit the wet way?

body.text: Arali ni na mbeu kana mitshelo tsini, fhambanyani tsumbo idzi u ya nga nḓila idzi mbili. Ṱalutshedzani phambano nga u amba uri mbeu i vha hani nga tshifhinga tsha khaṋo.
body.backTranslation: If you have seed or fruits nearby, separate these examples by these two ways. Explain the difference by saying how the seed is at the time of harvest.

english.heading: Process Dry Seed
body: Leave dry-seeded crops on the plant until the seed is fully mature.
Collect it before weather, birds or bursting pods take the harvest.
Remove chaff and damaged seed.
Then spread the clean seed in a single layer in moving air and shade.
What tells you that dry seed is mature enough to collect?
If you have a dry pod or seed head, handle it. Listen for the seed. Compare green, flexible plant material with brown, brittle material.
Wait for maturity. For final drying, use shade and airflow.

heading.text: U Lugisa Mbeu Yo Omaho

body.text: Litshani mbeu ya zwilimiwa zwa mbeu yo omaho (dry-seeded) kha tshimela u swika yo vhibva zwavhuḓi.
body.backTranslation: Leave seed of dry-seeded crops on the plant until it is fully ripe.

body.text: I kuvhanganyeni phanḓa ha uri mutsho (weather), zwiṋoni (birds) kana pod dzi vuleaho (bursting) zwi dzhie khaṋo.
body.backTranslation: Gather it before weather, birds or bursting pods take the harvest.

body.text: Bvisani chaff na mbeu yo tshinyalaho.
body.backTranslation: Remove chaff and spoiled seed.

body.text: Nga murahu, andadzani mbeu yo kunaho nga layer nthihi fhethu hune muya wa tshimbila na hune ha vha na murunzi.
body.backTranslation: Afterward, spread clean seed in one layer where wind moves and where there is shade.

body.text: Ndi mini zwine zwa ni sumbedza uri mbeu yo omaho yo vhibva lune ya nga kuvhanganywa?
body.backTranslation: What shows you that dry seed is ripe so that it can be gathered?

body.text: Arali ni na pod kana ṱhoho ya mbeu yo omaho, i fareni. Thetshelesani mbeu. Vhambedzani zwipiḓa zwa tshimela zwi sa athu u oma (green, flexible) na zwo omaho (brown, brittle).
body.backTranslation: If you have a pod or head of dry seed, hold it. Listen to the seed. Compare parts of the plant that are not yet dry (green, flexible) and dry ones (brown, brittle).

body.text: Lindelani u vhibva. Kha u omisa ha u fhedza, shumisani murunzi na muya (airflow).
body.backTranslation: Wait for ripeness. For the final drying, use shade and wind (airflow).

english.heading: Watch: Dry Processing
body: Allow the seed to mature on the plant before collecting it.
Watch how it is collected once mature. Chaff and debris are removed. Damaged seed is taken out.
The clean seed is then spread in a single layer in moving air and shade.
Follow the steps in order: mature, collect, clean, dry.
Think about where you could carry out each part of this process.

heading.text: Sedzani: U Lugisa Mbeu Yo Omaho

body.text: Litshani mbeu i vhibve kha tshimela phanḓa ha u i kuvhanganya.
body.backTranslation: Leave seed to ripen on the plant before gathering it.

body.text: Sedzani nḓila ine ya kuvhanganywa ngayo musi yo vhibva. Chaff na debris zwi a bviswa. Mbeu yo tshinyalaho i a bviswa.
body.backTranslation: Look at the way it is gathered when it is ripe. Chaff and debris are removed. Spoiled seed is removed.

body.text: Nga murahu, mbeu yo kunaho i andadzwa nga layer nthihi fhethu hune muya wa tshimbila hone na hune ha vha na murunzi.
body.backTranslation: Afterward, clean seed is spread in one layer where wind moves and where there is shade.

body.text: Tevhelani zwipiḓa izwi nga u tevhekana: u vhibva, u kuvhanganya, u kunakisa, u omisa.
body.backTranslation: Follow these steps in order: ripening, gathering, cleaning, drying.

body.text: Humbulani hune na nga ita hone tshipiḓa tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe tsha mushumo uyu.
body.backTranslation: Think where you could do each step of this work.

english.heading: Wet Processing for Tomato Seed
body: Scoop tomato seed and flesh into a clean jar with a little water.
Leave it open or loosely covered. Keep it out of direct sun.
After two to three days, a light film and a sour smell may appear.
Rinse promptly. Remove debris. Then spread the clean seed thinly to dry.
Do not seal an actively fermenting jar.
Think about the signs that tell you the process has begun. Also think about signs that would make you discard the batch.
Find a jar, a sieve and a drying plate. When you are ready, start a small batch. Remember the order: scoop, ferment briefly, rinse and dry completely.

heading.text: U Lugisa Mbeu ya Tamatisi nga Maḓi

body.text: Bvisani mbeu na nama ya tamatisi ni i vhee kha jara yo kunaho i re na maḓi maṱuku.
body.backTranslation: Take out the seeds and the flesh of the tomato and put it in a jar that is clean, which has little water.

body.text: Ni i litshe yo vulea kana yo fukedzwa zwiṱuku (loosely covered). Ni songo i vhea ḓuvhani (direct sun).
body.backTranslation: Leave it open or covered a little (loosely covered). Do not put it in direct sun.

body.text: Nga murahu ha maḓuvha mavhili kana mararu, film ṱhukhu na munukho wa u vhava (sour) zwi nga vhonala.
body.backTranslation: After two or three days, a thin film and a sour smell may appear.

body.text: Ṱanzwani nga u ṱavhanya. Bvisani debris. Nga murahu andadzani mbeu yo kunaho nga layer ṱhukhu (thinly) uri i ome.
body.backTranslation: Wash quickly. Remove debris. Afterwards spread clean seed thinly so that it dries.

body.text: Ni songo vala jara ine ya khou ita fermentation.
body.backTranslation: Do not close the jar that is fermenting.

body.text: Humbulani zwiga zwine zwa ni sumbedza uri fermentation yo thoma. Humbulani na zwiga zwine zwa nga ita uri ni pose tshigwada itsho.
body.backTranslation: Think of signs that show you that fermentation has begun. Think also of signs that could make you throw away that portion.

body.text: Wanani jara, sieve na plate ya u omisa. Musi no lugela, thomani tshigwada tshiṱuku. Humbulani u tevhekana: bvisani, itani fermentation tshifhinganyana, ṱanzwani ni omise zwo fhelelaho.
body.backTranslation: Find a jar, a sieve and a drying plate. When you are ready, begin a small portion. Think of the order: remove, ferment briefly, wash and dry completely.

english.heading: Watch: Wet Processing for Tomato Seed
body: Watch the whole process in order.
A ripe tomato is opened. The seed and gel are scooped into a clean jar. Only a little water is added.
The jar is left open or loosely covered for two to three days.
When a light film and sour smell appear, the contents are poured through a sieve. The seed is rinsed until it is clean.
Finally, the seed is spread in a single layer in the shade until completely dry.
Repeat the steps to yourself: scoop, ferment briefly, rinse, dry completely.

heading.text: Sedzani: U Lugisa Mbeu ya Tamatisi nga Maḓi
heading.backTranslation: Look: Preparing Tomato Seed with Water

body.text: Sedzani mushumo woṱhe nga u tevhekana.
body.backTranslation: Look at the whole work in order.

body.text: Tamatisi yo vhibvaho i a vulwa. Mbeu na gel zwi bviswa nga spoon zwa vhewa kha jara yo kunaho. Hu engedzwa maḓi maṱuku fhedzi.
body.backTranslation: A ripe tomato is opened. Seed and gel are removed with a spoon and put in a clean jar. Only a little water is added.

body.text: Jara i litshwa yo vulea kana yo fukedzwa zwiṱuku (loosely covered) lwa maḓuvha mavhili kana mararu.
body.backTranslation: The jar is left open or covered a little (loosely covered) for two or three days.

body.text: Musi film ṱhukhu na munukho wa u vhava (sour) zwi tshi vhonala, zwi re ngomu zwi shululelwa kha sieve. Mbeu i ṱanzwiwa u swika yo kuna.
body.backTranslation: When a thin film and a sour smell appear, what is inside is poured into a sieve. Seed is washed until it is clean.

body.text: Mafheleloni, mbeu i andadzwa nga layer nthihi murunzini u swika yo oma zwo fhelelaho.
body.backTranslation: In the end, seed is spread in one layer in shade until it is completely dry.

body.text: Dovhololani zwipiḓa izwi: bvisani, itani fermentation tshifhinganyana, ṱanzwani, omisani zwo fhelelaho.
body.backTranslation: Repeat these steps: remove, ferment briefly, wash, dry completely.

english.heading: Practical Activity
body: This is where the lesson leaves the screen and reaches your hands.
Start one real batch of wet-processed seed.
Use one ripe, healthy fruit, a clean jar, a spoon, a little water, a sieve and a drying plate.
Put the seed, flesh and a little water into the jar. Add a label with the date.
You will look after this jar after the lesson. Decide now when you will inspect it, when you will rinse it and when you will dry the seed.
Your jar needs a date and a return plan. Write down the date when you will inspect it after two days.

heading.text: Mushumo wa u Ita nga Zwanḓa

body.text: Hafha ndi hune ngudo ya bva kha screen ya swika zwanḓani zwaṋu.
body.backTranslation: Here is where the lesson leaves the screen and reaches your hands.

body.text: Thomani tshigwada tshithihi tsha vhukuma tsha mbeu ine ya lugiswa nga maḓi (wet-processed).
body.backTranslation: Begin one real portion of seed that is wet-processed.

body.text: Shumisani mutshelo muthihi wo vhibvaho, u re na mutakalo, jara yo kunaho, spoon, maḓi maṱuku, sieve na plate ya u omisa.
body.backTranslation: Use one ripe, healthy fruit, a clean jar, a spoon, a little water, a sieve and a drying plate.

body.text: Vheani mbeu, nama na maḓi maṱuku kha jara. Ṅwalani ḓuvha kha jara (label).
body.backTranslation: Place the seed, flesh and a little water in the jar. Write the date on the jar (label).

body.text: Ni ḓo ṱhogomela jara iyi nga murahu ha ngudo. Nangani zwino uri ni ḓo i sedza lini, ni ḓo ṱanzwa mbeu lini na uri ni ḓo i omisa lini.
body.backTranslation: You will look after this jar after the lesson. Choose now when you will look at it, when you will wash the seed and when you will dry it.

body.text: Jara yaṋu i ṱoḓa ḓuvha na pulane ya u vhuya. Ṅwalani ḓuvha ḽine na ḓo i sedza nga murahu ha maḓuvha mavhili.
body.backTranslation: Your jar needs a date and a plan of returning. Write the date on which you will look at it after two days.

english.heading: Dry First, Seal Later
body: Drying is not a decorative final step.
Moist seed keeps breathing. It can heat, rot or die in storage.
Use shade, moving air and time.
Seal seed only when you are sure it is dry.
Which place in your home has shade and airflow, but is protected from rain and cooking steam?
Choose one safe drying place. Then identify one unsafe place.
Repeat this to check your understanding: dry first, seal later.

heading.text: Omisani Mathomoni, Valani nga Murahu

body.text: U omisa a si tshipiḓa tsha u fhedza tshine tsha nga litshwa.
body.backTranslation: Drying is not a last step that can be left.

body.text: Mbeu i re na maḓi (moist) i kha ḓi fema. I nga fhisa, ya tshinyala (rot) kana ya fa musi i tshi vhulungwa.
body.backTranslation: Moist seed is still breathing. It can heat up, rot or die when it is stored.

body.text: Shumisani murunzi, muya u tshimbilaho na tshifhinga.
body.backTranslation: Use shade, moving wind and time.

body.text: Valani mbeu fhedzi musi no khwaṱhisedza uri yo oma.
body.backTranslation: Close the seed only when you have made sure that it is dry.

body.text: Ndi fhethu hufhio hayani haṋu hune ha vha na murunzi na muya, fhedzi ho tsireledzea kha mvula na steam ya u bika?
body.backTranslation: Which place at your home has shade and wind, but is protected from rain and cooking steam?

body.text: Nangani fhethu huthihi ha u omisa ho tsireledzeaho. Nga murahu ni bule fhethu huthihi hu sa tsireledzei.
body.backTranslation: Choose one protected drying place. Afterward open one unprotected place.

body.text: Dovhololani izwi u sedza arali ni tshi pfesesa: omisani mathomoni, valani nga murahu.
body.backTranslation: Repeat these to check if you understand: dry first, close afterward.

english.heading: Protect Seed from Heat, Light and Moisture
body: Paper packets breathe and organise seed. But they are not enough in a humid climate.
Once the seed is completely dry, place the labelled packets inside a sealed, moisture-proof container. If available, include a food-safe desiccant.
Keep the container as cool and dark as possible in your home.
Which room or cupboard in your home stays coolest and driest?
Compare a paper envelope on its own with an envelope inside a sealed container.
Safe storage has two layers: a labelled paper packet inside a dry, sealed container.

heading.text: Tsireledzani Mbeu kha U Fhisa, Tshedza na Maḓi
heading.backTranslation: Protect Seed from Heat, Light and Moisture

body.text: Pakete dza bammbiri dzi a fema nahone dzi dzudzanya mbeu. Fhedzi kha mutsho u re na maḓi manzhi (humid climate), a dzi tsireledzi mbeu zwo fhelelaho.
body.backTranslation: Paper packets breathe and organise seed. But in a humid climate, they do not fully protect seed.

body.text: Musi mbeu yo oma zwo fhelelaho, vheani pakete dzo ṅwalelwaho (labelled) ngomu ha container yo valiwaho ine maḓi a sa kone u dzhena khayo. Arali i hone, vheani na food-safe desiccant.
body.backTranslation: When seed is fully dry, put labelled packets inside a closed container that water cannot enter. If it is available, also put in food-safe desiccant.

body.text: Vhulungani container fhethu ho rotholaho na hu re na swiswi nga hune zwa konadzea hayani haṋu.
body.backTranslation: Keep the container in a cool, dark place as far as is possible at your home.

body.text: Ndi fhethu hufhio hayani haṋu (room kana cupboard) hune ha dzula ho rothola na u oma u fhira huṅwe?
body.backTranslation: Which place at your home (room or cupboard) stays cooler and drier than others?

body.text: Vhambedzani envelope ya bammbiri fhedzi na envelope i re ngomu ha container yo valiwaho.
body.backTranslation: Compare a paper envelope alone and an envelope that is inside a closed container.

body.text: U vhulunga ho tsireledzeaho hu na layers mbili: pakete ya bammbiri yo ṅwalelwaho (labelled) ngomu ha container yo omaho, yo valiwaho.
body.backTranslation: Protected storage has two layers: a labelled paper packet inside a dry, closed container.

english.heading: Label Every Packet
body: Storage protects the seed physically. Written information protects its meaning.
The packet must tell the next person what crop it is.
It must give the variety or local name.
It must say when the seed was saved and where it came from.
Which local names could be lost if you write only the crop name?
Take a blank packet. Practise writing the four pieces of information: crop, variety or local name, date and source.
Check again that all four are present.

heading.text: Ṅwalani kha Pakete Iṅwe na Iṅwe

body.text: U vhulunga hu tsireledza mbeu nga muvhili. Mafhungo o ṅwalwaho a tsireledza ṱhalutshedzo yayo.
body.backTranslation: Keeping protects seed physically. Written information protects its explanation.

body.text: Pakete i fanela u vhudza muthu a tevhelaho uri ndi tshilimiwa (crop) tshifhio.
body.backTranslation: A packet must tell the next person which crop it is.

body.text: I fanela u ṋea lushaka (variety) kana dzina ḽa henefho.
body.backTranslation: It must give the variety or the local name.

body.text: I fanela u amba uri mbeu yo vhulungwa lini na uri yo bva ngafhi.
body.backTranslation: It must say when the seed was kept and where it came from.

body.text: Ndi madzina afhio a henefho ane a nga xela arali ni tshi ṅwala dzina ḽa crop fhedzi?
body.backTranslation: Which local names could be lost if you write only the crop name?

body.text: Dzhiani pakete i si na tshithu. Lingedzani u ṅwala mafhungo maṋa: crop, lushaka (variety) kana dzina ḽa henefho, ḓuvha na hune ya bva hone.
body.backTranslation: Take an empty packet. Try to write four pieces of information: crop, variety or local name, date and where it came from.

body.text: Sedzani hafhu uri mafhungo oṱhe maṋa a hone.
body.backTranslation: Check again that all four pieces of information are there.

english.heading: Ten-Seed Germination Test
body: A seed packet can look perfect even when the seed is losing life.
Ten seeds make the calculation easy.
Keep them warm and moist. Do not submerge them in water.
Then count the normal seedlings.
Six out of ten is about sixty percent. That tells you to sow more heavily, use the seed only as a trial, or replace it.
If eight seeds out of ten germinate, what percentage is that?
The answer is eighty percent.
Start a ten-seed test with an old packet. Write down the date and the day when you will count.

heading.text: Mulingo wa U Mela wa Mbeu dza Fumi

body.text: Pakete ya mbeu i nga vhonala yavhuḓi naho mbeu i tshi khou fhelelwa nga vhutshilo.
body.backTranslation: A seed packet can look good even when the seed is losing life.

body.text: Mbeu dza fumi dzi ita uri mbalo i leluwe.
body.backTranslation: Ten seeds make counting easy.

body.text: Dzi vhulungeni fhethu hu dudelaho (warm) nahone hu re na maḓi (moist). Ni songo dzi vhea ngomu ha maḓi (submerge).
body.backTranslation: Keep them in a warm and moist place. Do not put them in water (submerge).

body.text: Nga murahu vhalani zwimela zwiṱuku (seedlings) zwi re na tshivhumbeo tshavhuḓi (normal).
body.backTranslation: Afterward count the seedlings that have a good form (normal).

body.text: 6 kha 10 ndi tsini na 60 phesenthe. Izwo zwi ni vhudza uri ni zwale mbeu nnzhi, ni shumise mbeu u linga fhedzi (trial), kana ni i shandukise nga iṅwe.
body.backTranslation: 6 of 10 is close to 60 percent. That tells you to plant more seed, to use the seed for a trial only, or to replace it with other seed.

body.text: Arali mbeu dza 8 kha dza 10 dzi tshi mela, ndi phesenthe ifhio?
body.backTranslation: If 8 of 10 seeds sprout, what percentage is it?

body.text: Phindulo ndi 80 phesenthe.
body.backTranslation: The answer is 80 percent.

body.text: Thomani mulingo wa mbeu dza 10 nga pakete ya kale. Ṅwalani ḓuvha ḽa ṋamusi na ḓuvha ḽine na ḓo vhala.
body.backTranslation: Begin a test of 10 seeds with an old packet. Write today's date and the date on which you will count.

english.heading: Watch: Ten-Seed Germination Test
body: Count exactly ten seeds.
Place them in two rows of five.
Keep them on moist paper or cloth. Do not submerge them in water.
After some time, count again.
Here, six have germinated. Four have not. The total is still ten.
The germination rate is therefore sixty percent.
Check yourself. Did you count ten at the start, six germinated seeds and four ungerminated seeds at the end?

heading.text: Sedzani: Mulingo wa U Mela wa Mbeu dza Fumi

body.text: Vhalani mbeu dza 10 fhedzi.
body.backTranslation: Count only 10 seeds.

body.text: Vheani mbeu nga mitevhe mivhili (rows), mbeu dza 5 kha muṅwe na muṅwe.
body.backTranslation: Place the seeds in two rows, 5 seeds in each.

body.text: Dzi vhulungeni kha bammbiri kana cloth zwi re na maḓi (moist). Ni songo dzi vhea ngomu ha maḓi (submerge).
body.backTranslation: Keep them in paper or cloth that is moist. Do not put them in water (submerge).

body.text: Nga murahu ha tshifhinga, vhalani hafhu.
body.backTranslation: After some time, count again.

body.text: Fhano, 6 dzo mela. 4 a dzo ngo mela. Tshivhalo tshoṱhe tshi kha ḓi vha 10.
body.backTranslation: Here, 6 sprouted. 4 did not sprout. The total is still 10.

body.text: Ngauralo, tshivhalo tsha u mela (germination rate) ndi 60 phesenthe.
body.backTranslation: Therefore, the germination rate is 60 percent.

body.text: Sedzani hafhu: naa no vhala 10 mathomoni, 6 dzo melaho na 4 dzi songo melaho mafheleloni?
body.backTranslation: Check again: did you count 10 at the beginning, and 6 that sprouted and 4 that did not sprout at the end?

english.heading: Share Seed with Its Information
body: A seed exchange is not a table of unknown packets.
A good exchange moves information with the seed.
It tells you what the seed is. Where it came from. When it was saved. And whether it has been tested.
This honesty strengthens the whole network.
What information would help you trust seed from another household?
Take one of your packets. Practise describing it before sharing it. Give the seed and its basic history together.

heading.text: Kovhelani Mbeu na Mafhungo Ayo

body.text: U kovhelana mbeu a si tafula ya pakete dzi sa ḓivhiwi.
body.backTranslation: Sharing seed is not a table of unknown packets.

body.text: U kovhelana havhuḓi hu tshimbidza mafhungo khathihi na mbeu.
body.backTranslation: Good sharing moves information together with seed.

body.text: Zwi ni vhudza uri mbeu ndi mini. Yo bva ngafhi. Yo vhulungwa lini. Na uri yo lingwa kana hai.
body.backTranslation: It tells you what the seed is. Where it came from. When it was kept. And whether it has been tested or not.

body.text: U fulufhedzea uhu hu khwaṱhisa vhathu vhoṱhe vha kovhelanaho mbeu.
body.backTranslation: This reliability strengthens all people who share seed.

body.text: Ndi mafhungo afhio ane a nga ni thusa u fulufhela mbeu i bvaho kha muṅwe muṱa?
body.backTranslation: Which information could help you trust seed that comes from another household?

body.text: Dzhiani iṅwe ya pakete dzaṋu. Lingedzani u i ṱalutshedza ni sa athu u i kovhela. Ṋeani mbeu khathihi na mafhungo ayo a ndeme (history).
body.backTranslation: Take one of your packets. Try to explain it before sharing it. Give the seed together with its important information (history).

english.heading: Field Assignment
body: This task is small enough to finish. It is important enough to matter.
Build one working seed-storage container.
Put labelled paper packets inside a dry, sealed container.
Take a photograph of it.
Then name the crop whose seed you will save this season.
The photograph is evidence. The packet is a beginning.
What do you still need to finish this at home?
Write a short materials list. Choose a completion date.

Before sealing the container, check your work: the seed is completely dry; every packet has the crop, variety and date; the container is cool, dark and protected from moisture; and you selected several healthy parent plants.

heading.text: Mushumo wa Tsimu

body.text: Mushumo uyu ndi muṱuku lune na nga u fhedza. Nahone u na ndeme.
body.backTranslation: This work is small so that you can finish it. And it has importance.

body.text: Lugisani container nthihi ya u vhulunga mbeu i shumaho.
body.backTranslation: Prepare one working container for keeping seed.

body.text: Vheani pakete dza bammbiri dzo ṅwalelwaho (labelled) ngomu ha container yo omaho, yo valiwaho.
body.backTranslation: Place labelled paper packets inside a dry, closed container.

body.text: Dzhiani tshifanyiso (photo) tshayo.
body.backTranslation: Take a picture (photo) of it.

body.text: Nga murahu ni bule tshilimiwa tshine na ḓo vhulunga mbeu yatsho khalaṅwaha iyi.
body.backTranslation: Afterward open the crop whose seed you will keep this year.

body.text: Tshifanyiso ndi vhuṱanzi. Pakete ndi mathomo.
body.backTranslation: A photo is proof. A packet is a beginning.

body.text: Ndi zwifhio zwine na kha ḓi zwi ṱoḓa u fhedza mushumo hayani?
body.backTranslation: What do you still need to finish the work at home?

body.text: Ṅwalani mutevhe mupfufhi wa zwishumiswa. Nangani ḓuvha ḽa u fhedza.
body.backTranslation: Write a short list of tools. Choose a date to finish.

body.text: Ni sa athu u vala container, sedzani: mbeu yo oma zwo fhelelaho; pakete iṅwe na iṅwe i na crop, lushaka (variety) na ḓuvha; container i swiswini, yo rothola, yo tsireledzea kha maḓi (moisture); no nanga zwimela zwinzhi zwa vhabebi zwi re na mutakalo.
body.backTranslation: Before closing the container, check: seed completely dry; every packet has crop, variety and date; the container is in the dark, cool, protected from moisture; you have chosen many healthy parent plants.

english.heading: Field Action
body: Select.
Process.
Protect.
Verify.
Those four actions carry a seed collection from this field into the next season.
Begin with one crop and do it well.
Which crop will you begin with?
Say it aloud. Then choose one action you will take next.
The next season is already inside the seed you choose today.

heading.text: Tshiito tsha Tsimu

body.text: Nangani.
body.backTranslation: Choose.

body.text: Lugisani (process).
body.backTranslation: Prepare (process).

body.text: Tsireledzani.
body.backTranslation: Protect.

body.text: Khwaṱhisedzani.
body.backTranslation: Verify.

body.text: Zwiito izwi zwiṋa zwi isa mbeu dzo kuvhanganywaho u bva kha tsimu iyi u ya kha khalaṅwaha i tevhelaho.
body.backTranslation: These four actions carry seed gathered from this field to the coming season.

body.text: Thomani nga tshilimiwa (crop) tshithihi ni zwi ite zwavhuḓi.
body.backTranslation: Begin with one crop (crop) and do it well.

body.text: Ndi tshilimiwa (crop) tshifhio tshine na ḓo thoma ngatsho?
body.backTranslation: Which crop (crop) will you begin with?

body.text: Zwi ambeni nga ipfi ḽihulu (aloud). Nga murahu ha izwo, nangani tshiito tshithihi tshine na ḓo tshi ita.
body.backTranslation: Say it with a big word/voice (aloud). After that, choose one action that you will do.

body.text: Khalaṅwaha i tevhelaho yo no vha ngomu ha mbeu ine na i nanga ṋamusi.
body.backTranslation: The coming season is already inside the seed that you choose today.
